papers.title: Quantifying within-category spillovers in retail promotions — Causal evidence from double machine learning
papers.authors: Cantalupo M., Silverio F.
papers.abstract: Promotional activities play a key role in retail marketing, yet their influence often extends beyond the promoted items. Quantifying these indirect effects within a product category is essential for effective pricing, shelf allocation, and inventory management, but remains challenging due to the complex interdependence of consumer responses. This study proposes a two-stage methodology for the causal estimation of within-category spillover effects generated by price promotions in retail environments. The first stage develops an advanced data processing framework to uncover many-to-one relationships between promoted and non-promoted products and to construct a feature-rich representation of observational retail data. This enables the second stage to causally estimate spillover effects through a DML approach, complemented by empirical diagnostic checks. The methodology is examined under three alternative DML specifications and evaluated using 42 months of daily data from the Carbonated Soft Drinks category of a large Italian grocery retailer. Results indicate that fully linear models fail to capture the complexity of promotional interactions, whereas flexible nonparametric approaches yield statistically significant effects generating average sales variations ranging from (Formula presented) to (Formula presented). The findings reveal predominantly negative spillovers, reflecting cannibalization and inter-brand competition in line with established marketing research, alongside limited evidence of complementarity under context-dependent conditions, as highlighted through model explainability analysis. Placebo permutation tests provide additional support against spurious findings in the observational setting. Overall, the study combines causal inference with explainable analytics, offering actionable insights for promotion management and category planning.

papers.title: Unsupervised feature selection via graph-based proximity and structured autoencoder-like NMF
papers.authors: Pakmanesh M., Saberi-Movahed F., Salemi A., Tiwari P.
papers.abstract: Most unsupervised feature selection (UFS) methods select discriminative features by using graph learning or matrix factorization techniques to generate pseudo-labels. However, existing methods suffer from two major limitations. First, graph learning-based approaches usually capture only first-order similarities and therefore fail to model higher-order relationships among data samples. Second, matrix factorization-based methods mainly focus on decoding, that is, reconstructing the data from latent factors, but they do not provide explicit encoding mechanisms for learning meaningful representations directly from the original features. To address these challenges, we propose UFS-GAN, a novelUFSmethod based onGraph-based proximity and structuredAutoencoder-likeNonnegative matrix factorization. UFS-GAN leverages non-negative spectral clustering for interpretable cluster discovery and adopts an encoder–decoder design: the encoder projects features into embeddings, and the decoder reconstructs features from them. This joint process integrates representation learning and interpretability within a unified model. UFS-GAN further incorporates a structured proximity matrix to adaptively integrate both first- and higher-order graph proximities, thereby capturing the intrinsic data structure more effectively. Simultaneously, it employs a complementary NMF-based encoder-decoder model that combines the encoding capacity of autoencoders with the interpretability and structured latent space of NMF, yielding more meaningful and interpretable feature representations. Finally, UFS-GAN unifies these two nonnegative embedding- and representation-based encoder-decoder models within a structured framework for feature selection. Experiments on ten benchmark datasets show that UFS-GAN reliably identifies discriminative features without class labels, outperforming several state-of-the-art UFS methods. Overall, UFS-GAN delivers consistent improvements, achieving on average nearly 6% higher accuracy than the strongest competing methods, with gains of up to about 9% on some datasets.

papers.title: AI ethics education: A scoping review of pedagogy, curriculum, and assessment
papers.authors: Hillis C., Bhattacharjee M., AlMousawi B., Martens R., Eltanahy T., Ono S., Hui M., Pham B., Swab M., Cormack G.V., Grossman M.R., Bagheri E., Marshall Z.
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in social and institutional decision-making, creating demand for ethically literate practitioners. Universities have responded by introducing AI ethics instruction, but the structure, content, pedagogy, and evaluation of these efforts remain unevenly documented.ObjectiveTo map and synthesize research on university level AI ethics education by characterizing course design, pedagogy, ethical themes, and assessment methods, and identifying evidence gaps that limit knowledge consolidation and instructional refinement.MethodsWe conducted a scoping review using Continuous Active Learning to screen 50,766 records up to 2024. 43 studies met inclusion after title, abstract, and full text review. We coded instructional design, curricular themes, pedagogical methods, and evaluation approaches using descriptive frequency counts and qualitative synthesis.ResultsMost included studies were conceptual or descriptive, with relatively few empirical evaluations. Instruction was concentrated in computing and engineering and primarily targeted undergraduate learners. Ethics content was more often embedded within technical courses than delivered as standalone offerings. Reported pedagogy relied heavily on lecture and case-based discussion, with fewer studies describing participatory formats such as simulations or role-play. Curricular emphasis clustered around bias/fairness and privacy, with comparatively less attention to governance, explainability, and trust. Evaluation most often relied on self-report and reflective methods, while validated instruments and performance-based assessments were less common, and behavioral or applied outcomes were rarely assessed.ConclusionsThe literature suggests a field oriented toward awareness-building more than measurable ethical competence. Clearer competency claims, stronger assessment transparency, and greater alignment between instructional design and evaluation would improve comparability across studies and support evidence-informed course development.

papers.title: Multi-domain generalization few-shot intent recognition with dual representation learning
papers.authors: Yanga S., Dua Y.
papers.abstract: Intent recognition stands as one of the key challenges in achieving high-quality human-computer interaction, with few-shot intent recognition specifically addressing data scarcity. Existing approaches assume either identical data domains or single-domain generalization, overlooking the inherent diversity of intent domains in real-world scenarios. Intent expressions across domains often exhibit significant differences, severely impairing a model’s recognition capability in new domains. However, existing methods focus solely on in-domain adaptation or cross-domain transfer, resulting in an isolation between in-domain and cross-domain representation learning. To address this, in this paper, we propose a novel Dual Representation Learning (DuRL) method that simultaneously enhances in-domain and cross-domain representation learning. DuRL improves accuracy for multi-domain generalization few-shot intent recognition by increasing the discriminative power of in-domain samples and reducing cross-domain representation differences. In the in-domain, DuRL utilizes the generalized knowledge from support instances to enhance the representations of query instances. Simultaneously, to reduce confusion between different class representations, we introduce class discrimination regularization to drive representations of distinct classes apart in feature space. In the cross-domain, DuRL employs representations from various domains to perform adversarial learning, thereby obtaining domain-invariant representations. During the adversarial process, the representations from different domains are pulled closer together to confuse the discriminator. In few-shot recognition, DuRL predicts the target class by computing the matching similarity between support and query instances. Theoretical proofs demonstrate the feasibility of enhancing in-domain generalization, while extensive experiments confirm that DuRL achieves state-of-the-art performance. Results show DuRL outperforms the SOTA by 4.39% and 2.15% on average in Clinic150 → Hwu64 of 10-way 1-shot and 3-shot scenarios, respectively.

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware significance and interaction-enhanced feature selection: A fuzzy multi-granularity information perspective
papers.authors: Wan J., Li X., Wang Z., Zhao J.
papers.abstract: Most existing information theoretic-based feature selection methods cannot effectively handle the uncertainty prevalent in data and often fall into the dilemma of feature correlation coupling. Motivated by these issues, this paper proposes an uncertainty-aware significance and interaction-enhanced feature selection (SIFS) approach. Specifically, a fuzzy multi-granularity space (FMGS) consisting of adaptive fuzzy neighborhood grains is first constructed, which is defined by a distributionally adaptive constraint set. Then, an uncertainty-aware fuzzy multi-granularity information uncertainty measures (FMIUMs) framework is established based on the adaptive fuzzy neighborhood grains in the FMGS. And the FMIUMs framework is used to characterize and capture feature correlations in the feature space, respectively. Moreover, significance and interaction are enhanced to design global weighting factors for features. Furthermore, a significance and interaction-enhanced feature selection (SIFS) approach with maximum relevance minimum class-constrained redundancy is proposed to excavate the most discriminative information in the feature space. The experimental comparison results with nine representative feature selection algorithms on fifteen datasets show that the proposed SIFS approach achieves the best classification performance and reduction effect, while statistical significance tests also demonstrate its significant advantages. Additionally, ablation experiment also validates the effectiveness of considering fuzzy multi-granularity information.

papers.title: Evolution of cooperation in public goods games on temporal higher‑order networks driven by utility and degree vectors
papers.authors: Wang X., Tu L., Wang X., Pan Y., Yu X., Huang Y.
papers.abstract: While higher-order networks offer a powerful framework to characterize population structure, a catalyst for cooperation, the existing Higher-Order Activity-Driven (HOAD) model, despite accounting for the temporal nature of interactions, overlooks individual adaptability and learning behaviors. To address this limitation, this paper integrates historical payoffs and interaction frequency into the generative mechanism of temporal higher-order networks and investigates the evolutionary dynamics of cooperation in Public Goods Games (PGG). Specifically, three novel network construction models and their algorithms are presented. These models, represented as temporal hypergraphs, are the Higher-Order Utility-Driven (HOUD) model driven by historical game utility vectors, the Higher-Order Degree-Driven (HODD) model driven by historical degree vectors, and the Higher-Order Utility-Degree-Driven (HO(U–D)D) model, which integrates both HOUD and HODD with a coordination factor. Then, Monte Carlo (MC) simulations explore the topological properties of the generated networks and the corresponding dynamics of cooperation in the PGG. Results show that, compared with the HOAD model, these three proposed models significantly enhance cooperation, increasing the final cooperation frequency from 0 to 0.12–0.84. They also dramatically lower the critical thresholds for both the enhancement factor and the maximum hyperedge size. Notably, the HODD model performs best, primarily due to its moderate levels of heterogeneity, sparsity, and clustering. Finally, according to the microscopic Markov chain approach (MMCA), the dynamical equations for the expected cooperation frequency are derived theoretically. Numerical simulations have verified that the MMCA theory results are in good agreement with the MC results.

papers.title: Understanding citation intents by generative intent model based on heterogeneous graph neural network
papers.authors: Phan T.A., Bui K.H.N., Jung J.J.
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel synthetic intent-based model for the citation intent classification, called SynIntent. Unlike prior works that treat citation contexts as plain text and rely on deep neural networks (including language models (LMs)) for representation learning, we investigate an unexplored information for this task: latent intent. To exploit these signals, we represent each citation context as a bipartite heterogeneous graph which composed of two node types: sentence nodes and latent intent nodes. Initial node representations are produced by a graph initialization module and subsequently refined through a graph attention network to capture sentence-intent dependencies, yielding a richer and more informative contextual representation. By leveraging latent intent information and sentence–intent relationships, SynIntent provides a novel, deeper and more holistic understanding of the semantic structure underlying citation contexts. The experiments on public datasets demonstrate that SynIntent outperforms the state-of-the-art models in both multiclass and multilabel classification scenarios. Specifically, we achieve a remarkable increase of 4.3% macro-F1 and 4.4% in accuracy on the ACL-ARC dataset. For the multilabel classification, we also observe improvements of 1% for strict metrics and 2% for weak metrics on the MultiCite dataset.

papers.title: Dual-stream multimodal shared prompt model for fake news detection
papers.authors: Liu S., Zeng H., Guo J., Zhang C., Lee I.K., Zhang Y., Li X.
papers.abstract: Current mainstream fake news detection methods primarily rely on pretrained models for encoding and feature extraction of both images and text, and then design interactive network modules based on the extracted features to achieve multimodal feature interaction. However, these interactions are often shallow and may not explore the complex relationships between image and text information, nor fully harness the potential of the advanced architecture of pretrained models. In response to these challenges, we propose a dual-stream multimodal shared prompt (DMSP) method based on pretrained models, which exploits the complementarity between image and text by introducing a learnable multimodal shared prompt into the image-text encoder. This enables the model to generate dual-stream deep image-text feature interaction vectors, maximizing the deep correlations and complementarity between image and text during the multimodal information interaction process. Furthermore, we design a pseudo-siamese attention network that learns multimodal interaction feature from two perspectives, local features and global features. This network effectively captures important interaction features, thereby enhancing the model’s ability to identify fake news. Finally, a classifier is used to perform binary classification on the dual-perspective deep image-text mixed features. Experimental results show that DMSP outperforms state-of-the-art baseline models with only five training epochs, achieving a 3.7% and 1% improvement in detection accuracy in the public PolitiFact and GossipCop datasets, respectively.

papers.title: Adaptive talent aligner: A large language model with dynamic hierarchical analysis and bias-corrective memory pool for personalized human resource management
papers.authors: Xu Y., Shi J., Zhou Y., Tian S., Zhang Z., Sun Z.
papers.abstract: As market competition intensifies and workforce scales grow, organizations increasingly seek precision in aligning role specifications with talent acquisition strategies. Employee-job alignment is a crucial aspect of strategic human resource management (HRM). Traditional methods, however, fall short in handling multi-criteria employee recommendations, adapting to dynamic preferences, and mitigating systemic biases. This study introduces a large language model (LLM)-enhanced framework that integrates dynamic hierarchical analysis with talent data retention mechanisms. A dynamic priority weight pool, based on traditional hierarchical analysis and utilizing text similarity matching, enables the LLM to efficiently access the importance matrix of skills required by the hierarchical analysis method. Simultaneously, the introduction of a bias-correction memory pool and preference aggregation pool enables the persistent storage of error correction memory and result expression bias. Leveraging the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve, a dynamic forgetting mechanism and a preference strength evaluation mechanism are developed to assess memory and preference strength, automatically eliminating redundant error correction and preference data to prevent data accumulation. Empirical evaluations show that this framework improves talent recommendation accuracy, customizes result presentation to align with institutional preferences, and reduces selection biases compared to traditional HRM systems, effectively tackling the complexities of modern workforce management.

papers.title: Waved zero streaming: A time series compression framework with adaptive segmentation optimization
papers.authors: Wang W., Chen W., Zhao H., Zhang Y., Lin M.
papers.abstract: The proliferation of time-series data from Internet of Things devices has made efficient compression mechanisms critical for large-scale data management. However, existing state-of-the-art algorithms often flounder when facing dynamic data fluctuations due to their reliance on rigid encoding strategies, while general-purpose compressors incur prohibitive latency. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces Wave Zero Streaming (WZS), a novel lossless compression framework specifically architected for non-stationary data streams. WZS synergizes three pivotal innovations: adaptive segmentation to isolate local fluctuation intensity, a heuristic genetic algorithm-based optimizer to fine-tune compression parameters dynamically, and a stream processing module enabling real-time adaptive algorithm selection. Extensive empirical evaluations across 43 diverse datasets reveal that WZS outperforms leading algorithms–including Camel, Chimp, and ACTF–achieving an average compression ratio improvement of 36.41% (peak: 53.08%), with a notable 13.28% enhancement specifically over the state-of-the-art Camel algorithm. Moreover, WZS surpasses general compression methods by 15.07% in compression ratio while reducing computational latency by two orders of magnitude, and exhibits a 16.45% speed advantage over comparable floating-point streaming baselines. These findings validate WZS as a scalable, high-performance solution that effectively balances efficiency and speed for resource-constrained IoT and edge computing environments.

papers.title: Local hyperplane-constrained self-representation for manifold clustering
papers.authors: Jia C., Huang C., Cai M., Ding W.
papers.abstract: To address the challenge of rejecting cross-manifold interference in non-linear data clustering, this paper proposes a novel method termed Local Hyperplane-Constrained Self-Representation for Manifold Clustering. By incorporating a local hyperplane constraint within each sample’s neighbors from other manifolds, the framework explicitly models local geometric separability to ensure that each sample is reconstructed primarily from points on the same manifold while suppressing neighbors from other manifolds. Theoretical analysis establishes error bounds for the model and provides a sufficient condition for manifold preservation, enhancing the method’s interpretability. Extensive evaluation on 12 synthetic and 10 real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms eleven state-of-the-art algorithms. Specifically, the method yields an average accuracy improvement of approximately 8%-15% over representative baseline methods, with gains exceeding 20% on certain datasets. Furthermore, the model achieves 100% clustering accuracy on the PIE dataset and demonstrates high computational efficiency by converging within just five iterations. The source code is available at https://github.com/HNU-MingjieCai/LHCMC.

papers.title: Beyond the prompt: Log-based threat detection and attribution for multi-Agent LLMs
papers.authors: Rabieinejad E., Zarrinkalam F., Dehghantanha A.
papers.abstract: Multi-agent large language models (LLMs) expand capability by delegating subtasks and invoking tools, but they also enlarge the attack surface with instruction-sensitive threats (e.g., prompt hijacking, retrieval poisoning, tool-use redirection) that unfold across agent-to-agent interactions and may look benign in text alone. We present ALTEDA, a log-based Threat Detection and Attribution framework for multi-agent LLMs that does not use user prompts or responses, reducing privacy risk while capturing cross-agent attack signals. ALTEDA red-teams a target workflow to collect synchronized application, network, and system logs, converts each run into an attributed directed multi-graph, and trains a graph-level detector which also supports early compromise detection from partial traces. In addition, our framework attributes detections back to responsible agents and interactions via SHAP with aggregator-aware redistribution. On a red-teamed multi-agent LLM system, we generate 800 traces with a 31.4% attack success rate and show that ALTEDA achieves strong end-to-end detection performance. Our result also shows ALTEDA can surface high-trust early alerts by around 40% trace progress and largely converges toward full performance by mid-trace, enabling intervention before attacks complete. Despite avoiding user content entirely, ALTEDA remains competitive with text-based detectors and incurs low computational overhead, making it suitable for real-time monitoring.

papers.title: Measuring stance dynamics in political debate using temporal graph neural networks
papers.authors: Zhou Z., Elejalde E.
papers.abstract: Social media users’ activity reflects their preferences and emotions. Mining stances from these digital traces helps predict public opinion and voting intent, but most existing approaches treat stance as static or short-term, overlooking how opinions evolve over extended periods. We introduce TWLGCN, a temporal graph neural network (GNN) that infers and tracks user-level stance dynamically from large-scale social media data with minimal manual annotation. Using Discrete-Time Dynamic Graphs (DTDGs), built from user-hashtag interactions, and integrating auxiliary user-user networks (e.g., retweets and mentions), TWLGCN aggregates current and historical signals to predict stance for all users at each period, including those not directly engaging with the target topic. Its training objective addresses class imbalance and applies a semi-supervised contrastive loss to improve representation quality. We evaluate TWLGCN on two large Twitter datasets covering the 2020 and 2022 Chilean constitutional referendums (over 1.2 million tweets from more than 17,000 users across 20 monthly periods). At each period, TWLGCN outperforms network-based baselines in macro-F1 by more than 5% using only 0.2% labeled hashtags. Beyond predictive gains, the proposed framework delivers interpretable, multi-granular insights into stance dynamics, revealing temporal drifts and group-level correlations. These results show that TWLGCN contributes to stance inference and user modeling for dynamic social platforms and is applicable to other evolving online contexts.

papers.title: Synthetic data generation: A tertiary study
papers.authors: Nobani N., Officioso G., Pallucchini F., Sperlì G., Mercorio F.
papers.abstract: Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) is expanding rapidly, yet existing surveys differ widely in scope and methodological quality. This tertiary study systematically searched four major scholarly databases (2015-2025) and, after PRISMA screening and DARE-4 appraisal,11https://www.york.ac.uk/crd/ identified 17 eligible secondary studies. The evidence reveals a strong concentration in healthcare (58.8% of surveys), limited coverage of non-health domains, and inconsistent reporting of evaluation protocols (e.g., incomplete specification of metrics, data splits, baselines, or evaluation scripts). Fidelity and downstream utility dominate assessment practices, whereas privacy and diversity remain under-examined. Only 4 of 17 surveys provide any reproducibility artefacts. By consolidating these findings, we propose a compact, domain-agnostic evaluation baseline and highlight structural gaps in transparency, domain breadth, and methodological consistency. The study offers actionable guidance for strengthening reproducibility and broadening the evidential foundations of SDG research.
